tickets.title: Cut the time tasks spend waiting on tests: CI runs the full suite once in parallel, workers stop duplicating it locally
tickets.asked:
Repository: JKershaw/LinearViewer.

## Why

About a third of a code task's working time is spent waiting on tests. That figure comes from 38 tasks and 333 worker dispatches (7–12 Nov), set against 600 PR CI runs:

* **Waiting on CI: 28%** of worker time. The median task waits about 24 min, across three CI waits: implementation, leftover and close-out.
* **Local full unit-suite runs: 10–13%.** That is about one run per implementation dispatch, at roughly 4–6 min each.

Most of that is duplication, not added assurance:

* CI's unit job runs the full unit suite twice, one pass after the other, at about 4 min each. That makes it the critical path, at about 8.5 min per run; no E2E shard takes more than about 5.5 min.
* Workers then run the same suite again locally before pushing. Merging is gated on `ci-success`, so the local run adds no quality. It only finds a failure sooner.
* One unit test, "without acorn" in the code-shape kit, fails on the runner machine every time because of its folder layout. In 8 of the 38 tasks a worker stopped to prove it also fails on main.

A subset of tests isn't the answer for code changes. An affected-tests selection over the last 60 merged PRs still needed about 82% of the suite's time, because about 990 of 1,254 unit test files reach the server. It would have caught 10 of 10 recent CI unit failures, so a subset is safe; it just isn't faster. LIN-4125 (2 Nov) reached the same pre-push conclusion, but its rule never reached the implementation template.

## What's wanted

1. **CI gives the same proof in less time.** Every check CI runs today still runs, but a PR's run finishes in roughly the time of its slowest single job, not the sum of the two unit passes.
2. **Workers stop running the full unit suite locally as a matter of routine.** Before pushing, a worker runs the tests that bear on its change, and CI is the full proof. This is said once, where the implementation stage gets its instructions, so it stops being re-decided per task.
3. **A local unit run is green on main on the runner machine,** so a red result means the change broke something.

## Done when

* A PR's CI wall time drops clearly below today's \~8.5 min median, with no check removed or weakened.
* New implementation trails show targeted local runs and CI as the full check, with no routine local full-suite run.
* The "without acorn" test passes on the runner machine, or is fixed so it no longer depends on where the temp folder sits.
* A re-measure on a fresh sample of tasks shows how much the test-wait share fell from about a third.

## Out of scope

* Building a test-selection tool for code changes. The evidence says it would save about a minute a run.
* Changing which tests exist, or loosening any of them.
tickets.done_when: PR CI wall time drops clearly below the ~8.5 min median with no check removed; implementation trails show targeted local runs; the 'without acorn' test passes on the runner; a fresh-sample re-measure shows the test-wait share fell.

tickets.title: The loop works on Jira: Harbour can create Jira issues, and Jira can hold a task's sealed words
tickets.asked:
**Repository:** JKershaw/LinearViewer (Harbour).

**What this is for.** The first outside test will be a small team on Jira who already use agents and are looking to have agents build their product. John has used Harbour on Jira for a few weeks: "it's mostly fine except for the gaps that you've identified." The gaps:

* Harbour can't create a Jira issue, so on Jira the loop can't file a task with the person's words sealed, mint a Periodical, or file what a task's last step files;
* Jira can't yet hold the block that keeps the person's words exactly as asked.

**What we want.** On a Jira-backed workspace, the loop does what it does on Linear: a task can be filed with the person's words sealed, a Periodical can be minted, and a task's last step can file what it files. It's checked on John's own Jira, which is already in real use.

**Done when** on John's Jira a task filed through Harbour keeps the person's words sealed, a Periodical mints, and a task's last step can file.

**Every change names what it retires. Questions:** settle engineering questions yourself; only John's calls (product, money, authority, what to retire) go to him as rulings.

tickets.title: The front end, left simpler: pages become modules that import what they share, one view at a time
tickets.asked:
**Repository:** JKershaw/LinearViewer (Harbour).

**What this is for.** John: "the UI issues trace back to one of my very first rules: no build step… it's the biggest target of the Theseus method… We don't need to tidy it all, but it's a perfect example where we can leave it better than we found it." The first slice (LIN-4446) served a pure server file to the browser at `/shared/` and retired the browser's copy. Its blind read found the cost: a bridge turns the shared file back into a global, with a load-timing rule that four files explain and nothing checks, and a second shared file would need a second bridge. On the direction, John: "I feel there's a sensible engineering approach, that a skilled developer would take… Excellent, that sounds like a great solution." Today the browser area has 44 script files that share through globals, `public/common.js` is 3,309 lines and `public/observation.js` 5,019, over 100 unit test files load browser scripts as classic scripts, and the area's note holds 10 Waiting entries.

**What we want.**

* Pages become ES modules that import what they share, as browsers do natively. Still no build step and no framework.
* Shared logic is imported, not restated: each converted view drops its copies.
* A bridge back to a global is only a temporary ramp for pages not yet converted: one at most, and visibly shrinking.
* The tests get simpler as views convert, not more elaborate.
* Taken one view at a time, each piece finishing one move and naming what it retired. John on size: "Happy for it to be whatever size is natural."
* No view is retired unless John rules it. The side rail and the visual refresh (LIN-4342, LIN-4343) come after, on the cleaner code.

**Done when**

* the slice 1 bridge is gone, or the only one left and shrinking under a check;
* the area's Waiting entries are settled, or say why not;
* the area reads better in a blind read after this work than before it, by more than an untouched area read at the same times.

**Every change names what it retires. Questions:** settle engineering questions yourself; only John's calls (product, money, authority, what to retire) go to him as rulings.
tickets.done_when: The slice-1 bridge is gone or the only one left and shrinking under a check; the area's Waiting entries are settled or say why not; the area reads better in a blind read than an untouched control area.
